places.name: Tromsø
places.intro: Norway’s largest city above the Arctic Circle, with a busy airport and many tour operators.
places.tip: On the coast the weather changes quickly. Tours often drive inland to look for gaps in the cloud, so a guided night can help even if you have a car.

places.name: Abisko
places.intro: A small village in Swedish Lapland at the edge of Abisko National Park, on the railway line between Kiruna and Narvik.
places.tip: There is very little artificial light, and the national park is right next to the village.

places.name: Rovaniemi
places.intro: The capital of Finnish Lapland, right on the Arctic Circle, with an airport served by winter flights from across Europe.
places.tip: The town is bright at night. Go a few kilometres out, to a lake shore or a clearing, for darker skies.

places.name: Reykjavík
places.intro: Iceland’s capital, where most visitors to the country stay.
places.tip: City lights wash out faint aurora. Þingvellir National Park, about 40 km away, or any dark stretch of coast is a far better place to wait.

places.name: Fairbanks
places.intro: A city in interior Alaska, far from the coast.
places.tip: Being inland, winter nights are very cold. Dress for well below freezing.

places.name: Yellowknife
places.intro: The capital of Canada’s Northwest Territories, on the north shore of Great Slave Lake.
places.tip: Winter nights are very cold. Several operators run heated viewing cabins outside town.

places.name: Inverness
places.intro: The main town of the Scottish Highlands.
places.tip: Scotland only sees the aurora during stronger geomagnetic storms, low in the northern sky. Treat it as a bonus, not a reason to travel; watch the NOAA forecast and look north from somewhere dark.
